nob0: 2026 Nobel Prizes: Optogenetics, One-Handed Molecules, IceCube | İhsan Eren
nob1: The 2026 Nobel Prizes in plain language: optogenetics, which switches brain cells on with light; the chemistry of one-handed molecules; and cosmic neutrinos caught in the ice of the South Pole. With animations, and a look at yesterday and tomorrow.
nob4: This year’s Nobel Prizes went to three questions: Can we talk to a single cell in the brain? Why does life always use just one hand? Can we get news from the far side of the universe? I have tried to explain all three simply enough to read over a cup of tea.
nob13: Karl Deisseroth · Peter Hegemann · Georg Nagel
nob14: “for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics”
nob15: In one sentence: A protein that lets a pond alga sense light was placed into brain cells; we can now switch chosen cells on and off with light, with a precision of one thousandth of a second.
nob16: Brain cells talk to each other with tiny electrical signals. In the cell’s membrane there are proteins that work like doors; when a door opens, charged particles rush in and the cell “fires”.
nob17: For years the problem was this: among billions of cells, how do we activate only the ones we want? An electrode stimulates every cell around it at once, and a drug is slow.
nob18: The answer came from a wholly unexpected place: a single-celled green alga living in pond water. This alga swims towards light because its membrane carries a door that opens when light touches it. Hegemann and Nagel found this door and showed how it works. Deisseroth and his team then placed its gene into nerve cells: the blue light came on, and the cell fired.
nob21: Above is the outside of the cell, below the inside. Blue light opens the door in the middle, charged particles rush in and the cell fires. Try it: one signal with every tap.
nob23: 2002–2003: The alga’s light-gated doors (channelrhodopsins) were described. 2005: The door was placed into rat nerve cells; the cells fired within milliseconds of blue light.
nob24: Laboratories around the world use this method to map which circuits sleep, memory, fear, pain and movement run through. It is one of the key tools for understanding conditions such as Parkinson’s disease and depression at the level of circuits.
nob26: In 2021, a patient who had lost his sight to retinitis pigmentosa was able to notice, count and touch objects in front of him again, thanks to a light-gated door placed in his eye and a special pair of goggles. This was a single patient and the vision was partial; studies are continuing.
nob27: What it means for humanity: We no longer just watch the brain; we can ask it a question and get an answer. In Deisseroth’s words: “We’re not using light to collect information, we’re using light to cause things to happen.”
nob30: “for the discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis”
nob31: In one sentence: They showed how to make only one of two mirror-image molecules, and even how a tiny difference can amplify itself.
nob32: Look at your hands: they are mirror images of each other, yet a right-hand glove will not fit the left hand. Many molecules also come in two such forms, “right-handed” and “left-handed”. The same atoms, the same bonds; the only difference is the mirror image.
nob33: The body notices the difference at once: one hand of the same molecule smells of spearmint, the other of caraway. It is the same with medicines. More than half of the medicines we use are “handed” molecules like this, and often only one hand does the job.
nob34: Here is the strange part: in the laboratory, an ordinary reaction makes equal amounts of both hands. Living things, however, always use just one; the building blocks of our proteins are left-handed, and the sugars in our DNA are right-handed. How did this preference begin? The question had gone unanswered for more than a hundred years.
nob35: A right and a left mitten are mirror images, yet they do not sit on top of each other: the thumbs end up on opposite sides.
nob37: In 1986 Henri Kagan showed something surprising: even when the helper molecule that steers a reaction (the catalyst) was not completely pure, the product could come out almost pure. The reason is that the helpers go around in pairs; when a right and a left pair up, that pair falls asleep.
nob38: If three quarters of the helpers are right-handed and one quarter left-handed, the pairs are split like this:
nob42: Three quarters of the mixture was right-handed; nine out of ten of the pairs at work turned out right-handed.
nob43: Soai: A difference that multiplies itself
nob44: In 1995 Kenso Soai went a step further: he found a reaction in which the product helps to make copies of itself. If there is an excess of one hand at the start, too small to see, the difference grows with every round.
nob48: The two hands are almost equal. The excess of one hand is only 0.00005%.
nob49: Excess 57%: about 79 of every 100 molecules now have the same hand.
nob50: Excess 99%: almost all of the molecules have the same hand.
nob51: 1848: While sorting crystals one by one with tweezers, Louis Pasteur realised that molecules can come in two “hands”. 1986: Kagan showed the non-linear effect; 1995: Soai showed the reaction that multiplies itself.
nob52: Making only the right hand of medicine, scent and flavour molecules is now everyday work for the chemical industry. Kagan’s finding showed that a pure product can be obtained even with a helper that is not completely pure.
nob53: The question of why life chose one hand can now be studied by experiment: a tiny accident, through a reaction that multiplies itself, could turn into the preference of a whole world. This is an important clue about how life began; it is not a final answer.
nob54: What it means for humanity: That the medicine you take is of the right “hand” is the work of this chemistry. In the words of Heiner Linke, chair of the prize committee, the two scientists “have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously.” Henri Kagan received the prize at the age of 95.
nob57: “for decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin”
nob58: In one sentence: With a giant detector buried in the ice of the South Pole, he managed to catch “ghost” particles coming from the most violent events in the universe.
nob59: Neutrinos are particles that interact with almost nothing. Right now, trillions of them pass through your body every second and you feel nothing. They pass straight through stars, and even through the whole Earth, without stopping.
nob60: That makes them unique messengers: they set out from places light cannot escape and reach us in a straight line. For the same reason they are very hard to catch.
nob61: Halzen’s idea was this: very rarely, a neutrino does hit an atom and gives off a small flash of blue light. To see that light you need a medium that is very large, very clear and very dark. The ice of the South Pole is exactly that. Holes reaching about 2.5 kilometres down were melted into the ice with hot water, and thousands of light sensors were lowered into them. A cubic kilometre of ice became a telescope.
nob63: Above is the surface of the South Pole, below the strings of sensors deep in the ice. The neutrino arrives unseen and hits an atom; the sensors see the blue light of the resulting particle one after another, which gives away the direction it came from.
nob64: 1930: Wolfgang Pauli predicted a particle that even he thought would never be caught. In 1956 the first neutrino was caught. In the late 1980s Halzen proposed turning the ice into a detector; IceCube was completed in 2011.
nob65: 2013: The first high-energy neutrinos from far beyond the Solar System were found. Then the sources began to appear: a giant black hole at the centre of a distant galaxy, the galaxy NGC 1068 and, in 2023, our own Milky Way.
nob66: A detector eight times larger (IceCube-Gen2) has been proposed. By reading light, gravitational waves and neutrinos together, the most violent events in the universe will be followed with different “senses”.
nob67: What it means for humanity: A completely new way of looking at the sky. For thousands of years we looked with light alone; now we can also read messengers that have travelled straight through matter. Halzen’s admission shows the human side of it: “Very few thought it would work, including myself.” After the prize he turned to his team of 450 scientists from 14 countries: “It’s a great relief for me to finally deliver the recognition that this great collaboration deserves.”
nob70: How does a pond alga see light? Why does this reaction not add up? Would anything glow at the bottom of the ice? On the day they were asked, none of these three questions looked as if it would ever ease anyone’s troubles. Nobody started studying algae saying “I am going to treat blindness”.
nob71: The time in between is worth a thought too: more than twenty years passed from the discovery of the alga’s door to the prize, and forty years from Kagan’s finding. Science is mostly a marathon; the prize is the photograph taken at the finish line.
nob72: As a physiotherapist, the one closest to me is the door opened by light: part of the knowledge we lean on when rebuilding movement after a stroke or in Parkinson’s disease comes from the maps of brain circuits drawn with this method.
nob73: A small question asked with patience may one day touch the life of someone we have never met.
nob75: It is a method of placing a light-sensitive protein into nerve cells and switching them on and off with light. This lets researchers test directly what a particular group of cells in the brain does.
nob76: Is optogenetics used as a treatment in people?
nob77: It is not yet a routine treatment. In 2021, partial recovery of vision was reported in one patient who had lost his sight to retinitis pigmentosa; clinical studies are continuing. Today the method is used mainly in research laboratories.
nob78: What does it mean for a molecule to be “right-handed” or “left-handed”?
nob79: Some molecules, just like a right and a left hand, cannot be laid on top of their mirror image; this is called chirality. The two forms are made of the same atoms but can behave differently in the body. That is why obtaining the right form matters in making medicines.
nob80: What is a neutrino, and is it harmful?
nob81: A neutrino is a fundamental particle with no electric charge and a very small mass. Trillions of them pass through our bodies every second; because they hardly interact with matter at all, they do us no harm.
